page: Amazon Web Services r7iz.12xlarge is a memory-optimized instance built on the AWS Nitro System. It features 48 vCPUs powered by dedicated Intel Xeon 6455B processors running at a high clock speed of 3.9 GHz. The instance is equipped with 384.0 GB of high-speed DDR5 memory operating at 5 GHz, providing 8.0 GB of RAM per physical core. It does not include local storage or dedicated GPU hardware, relying instead on network-attached storage and a baseline network bandwidth of 25 Gbps.

The hardware configuration delivers strong memory and compute performance. In benchmark testing, the instance achieved a top-tier single-core Geekbench score of 2278.0 and a strong multi-core score of 19792.0. Memory bandwidth is highly efficient, reaching 4250.25 GB/sec for cached small-block reads and 244.1 GB/sec for uncached large-block reads. The processor's support for Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX) and AVX-512 enables accelerated execution of vector and matrix operations, as demonstrated by a strong Passmark extended instructions score of 67129.65 and prompt processing speeds of 268.51 tokens per second for a medium 7B LLM.

From a qualitative cost-efficiency perspective, the r7iz.12xlarge offers a high-density memory profile combined with high-frequency compute cores, reducing the need to over-provision vCPUs solely to obtain sufficient RAM. This resource balance makes it highly suitable for memory-intensive workloads that also require significant CPU performance. Recommended workloads include in-memory databases like Redis, which achieved 65.52 million operations per second in testing, relational database operations, software compilation, and CPU-based machine learning inference.

The integration of Intel AMX and AVX-512 instruction sets enhances its capability for complex mathematical operations. Qualitatively, the instance provides high resource density for workloads requiring both high-frequency processing and large memory capacity. It is highly suited for in-memory databases, enterprise relational databases, software compilation, and CPU-based machine learning inference.
